gather.title: Why teams look for a Gather alternative
body: Gather made the virtual office popular, and for years a small team could use it for free. On September 15, 2025 that ended: Gather moved to $15 a member a month, or $12 billed yearly, and closed free offices that didn't upgrade. Teams that had locked in the old yearly price of $5.95 kept it until September 2026, so many of them are meeting the new price at this year's renewal.

Price isn't the only reason. Gather 2.0 is a new platform, and moving to it means building your office again. And many teams find they use a fraction of what they pay for: they want to see who's around, talk without scheduling, and meet. That's what the alternatives below are judged on.

items.title: TinyFloor
items.detail: $29 a month for the whole team, free for up to 3
items.body: A pixel-art office that opens in a browser tab, on a laptop or a phone. You see who's at their desk, walk up to talk, and step into the meeting room for video and screen sharing; there's team chat and a desk of your own. One price covers everyone you invite. It has no office editor, recordings, transcription or single sign-on, so teams that rely on those should look at Gather or Kumospace.

items.title: SoWork
items.detail: Basic $5.40 a member a month billed yearly; free for up to 10
items.body: The cheapest per-person plan here, and the most generous free plan for a team: up to 10 members, with meetings capped at 30 minutes. It's priced per member, so the bill grows with the team.

items.title: Kumospace
items.detail: Business from $16 a user a month; free for up to 5 members
items.body: A polished virtual office with desktop and mobile apps as well as the browser. Its free plan fits 5 members, 50 guests and one floor. For a team of 8 it's the most expensive option on this list after Gather's monthly plan.

items.title: WorkAdventure
items.detail: Business from $9 a user a month; free for up to 10 at once
items.body: Another pixel-art office, and open source, so a technical team can customise the map. Its free plan counts people online at the same time, up to 10, rather than members.

items.title: Teamflow
items.detail: $15 a person a month billed yearly; free for up to 5
items.body: A virtual office that runs as a desktop app for Mac and Windows, with mobile in beta. The free plan fits 5 people with 45-minute meetings. Billed yearly, it costs more per person than Gather's $12.

items.title: Roam
items.detail: A monthly price per active member; 14-day trial
items.body: A virtual office bundled with AI tools, in a desktop app you download. It charges only for members who are active, and has no free plan.

items.title: Discord
items.body: Not a virtual office, but many small teams already use its voice channels as one: drop in, talk, leave. It's free and the audio is good. It was built for gaming communities, so there's no office to see who's around, and work lives next to everything else on it.

items.title: Count the people who'll really use it
items.body: Free plans stop at 3 to 10 people, and most paid plans charge each person. For a team of 4 to 15, a flat price or a free plan that fits often beats a price per head.

items.title: Browser or app
items.body: Browser-only products need nothing installed and work for guests and contractors straight away. Desktop apps can do more, but everyone has to install them.

items.title: List your must-haves first
items.body: If you need recordings, transcripts, an office you design yourself or single sign-on, that narrows the list to Gather, Kumospace and a few others, whatever the price.

items.title: Try it on a normal working day
items.body: These tools prove themselves in the small moments: a quick question, a meeting that starts on time. A week of real work tells you more than a demo.

virtualOffice.title: What a virtual office is, and isn't
body: "Virtual office" means two different things. One is a business address: a service that gives a company a mailing address and sometimes a phone line, without a desk. The other, and the one this page is about, is an online office where a remote team works together during the day.

That second kind is a shared space that stays open while people work. Instead of a grid of faces that ends when a meeting does, everyone has a place in the office, can see who else is around, and starts a conversation the way you would in a building: by going over to someone.

items.title: See who's in
items.body: Everyone appears in the office, with a status, so you know who's at their desk, who's busy and who's in a meeting before you interrupt.

items.title: Talk without scheduling
items.body: Walk up to a teammate and start talking. A two-minute question stays two minutes, instead of becoming a calendar invite for tomorrow.

items.title: Meet in a room
items.body: Group conversations happen in a meeting room you walk into, with video and screen sharing, and you walk out when it's done.

items.title: Have a desk of your own
items.body: A desk gives each person a place, so the office looks like a team rather than a lobby.

items.title: Chat beside it
items.body: Messages and channels sit next to the floor, for what doesn't need talking.

virtualOffice.title: A virtual office next to the tools you already have
body: A virtual office doesn't replace video calls or team chat. It covers the part of the day neither was built for.

items.title: Small remote teams
items.body: Four to fifteen people who don't share a building, and miss being able to turn around and ask.

items.title: Startups
items.body: Early teams that decide things quickly and can't wait a day for the next meeting.

items.title: Agencies and studios
items.body: People who move between client projects all day and need to find each other fast.

items.title: Engineering and design teams
items.body: Pairing, reviewing and showing work on screen without booking a call for it.

items.title: Teams onboarding someone
items.body: A new hire can see who's around and ask, instead of guessing who is free to message.

virtualOffice.title: Setting one up in a day

items.title: Make the office
items.body: Name it after the team. There's nothing to design: the floor, desks and meeting room are ready.

items.title: Invite everyone with one link
items.detail: Paste it where the team already talks
items.body: Teammates sign in with Google or email and walk in. No install, on a laptop or a phone.

items.title: Everyone takes a desk
items.body: Once people sit somewhere, the office reads like a team and it's easy to find each other.

items.title: Hold the next standup in the meeting room
items.body: Moving one daily meeting into the office is what brings people back the next day.

items.title: Leave it open for a week
items.body: It proves itself in the small moments: a quick question answered in a minute, a conversation you overheard and joined.

virtualOffice.title: What makes a team keep using it

items.title: Keep it in a pinned tab
items.body: The office works when it's where you are, not one more thing to open.

items.title: Drop in, cameras optional
items.body: Voice first is fine; video is there when it helps. Nobody should feel watched.

items.title: Never use it to monitor people
items.body: A virtual office is a place to find each other, not a timesheet. Use it to check on people and it stops being a place anyone wants to be.

items.title: Meet there too
items.body: If the standup and the quick questions happen in the office, people come back to it without being asked.

discord.title: Why teams use Discord as an office
body: Plenty of small teams, especially developers, studios and startups, run their day in Discord. They make a server, open a voice channel, and people drop in and out the way they would walk into a shared room. It's free, the audio is good, screen sharing works in voice channels, and there's nothing new to learn for anyone who already uses it.
What it shows is that being one click from each other works better than scheduling every conversation. The question is whether an app built for gaming communities is the best home for that.

discord.title: Where it falls short for work

items.title: It's personal, not your company's
items.body: People join with their own Discord accounts, so work sits next to their gaming servers and friends, with every notification in one place.

items.title: Channels instead of a place
items.body: You see who's in which voice channel, but not who's at their desk and free for a minute. Joining a channel is an all-or-nothing way to start talking.

items.title: No obvious meeting room
items.body: A meeting is another voice channel. It works, but there's no sense of stepping into a room and back out to your desk.

items.title: Built around communities
items.body: Roles, servers and bots are made for large groups of strangers. A team of eight needs much less, and more of what an office has.

discord.title: If you stay on Discord, set it up like an office

items.title: Name voice channels after places
items.body: "Desks", "Meeting room" and "Focus" tell people what joining means, better than "General 1" and "General 2".

items.title: Agree what a status means
items.body: Do not disturb means heads-down; idle means away from the desk. Shared rules make it safe to drop in.

items.title: One text channel per project
items.body: Keeps work out of the general channel and easy to find later.

items.title: Keep a separate server for work
items.body: So the team's space doesn't mix with everyone's communities.

discord.title: When Discord is the better fit

items.title: Your team is already there and happy
items.body: If it works and nobody misses anything, there's no reason to move.

items.title: You run a community too
items.body: If customers or players are in the same server, Discord is built for exactly that.

items.title: Cost has to be zero
items.body: Discord is free for any number of people; TinyFloor is free for 3.

items.title: Make an office
items.body: Name it, and the floor, desks and meeting room are ready.

items.title: Share the invite link in your Discord
items.body: People sign in with Google or email and walk in from the browser.

items.title: Move the daily standup first
items.body: Hold it in the meeting room for a week while everything else stays where it is.

items.title: Then decide what stays
items.body: Many teams keep Discord for their community and use the office for the working day.

kumospace.title: Why small teams look for a Kumospace alternative

items.title: The free plan stops at 5
items.body: A sixth person means moving everyone to Business, and Business bills at least 5 members, so the first paid month for a team of 6 is $96 on a yearly plan or $120 monthly.

items.title: Free spaces are public
items.body: Kumospace lists the free plan as a public space. Restricting who can enter, with a password or by email, comes with Business.

items.title: Guests run on a clock
items.body: Guests can stay up to 4 hours a week. A freelancer or client who works with you every day has to become a paid member.

items.title: Per-member pricing grows with the team
items.body: Every hire adds $16 to $20 a month, including people who only drop in now and then.

items.title: Spaces you design
items.body: Furniture, flooring, decor, and activities like games, whiteboards and YouTube screens. If you want the office to look like your brand, Kumospace gives you far more to work with.

items.title: Recording
items.body: Business records meetings and presentations to share later. TinyFloor doesn't record.

items.title: Desktop and mobile apps
items.body: Kumospace has apps for Windows, macOS, iOS and Android as well as the browser. TinyFloor runs only in the browser.

items.title: Room for larger organizations
items.body: Several floors, user roles, unlimited chat history and, on Enterprise, single sign-on, a custom domain and an uptime SLA.

items.title: TinyFloor, for a small team
items.body: For a team of 4 to 15 that mainly needs to see who's in, talk without scheduling and meet in a room, and would rather pay one price than count seats.

items.title: Kumospace, for a designed space
items.body: If you want to design and brand the space, record meetings or use native apps, or a larger company needs single sign-on and analytics.

items.title: Kumospace free, for 5 or fewer
items.body: If a public space is fine and nobody needs to visit as a guest for more than 4 hours a week, the free plan may be all you need.

items.title: Make an office
items.body: Name it after the team. The floor, desks and meeting room are ready; there's nothing to rebuild.

items.title: Share one invite link
items.body: Teammates sign in with Google or email and walk in from the browser, on a laptop or a phone.

items.title: Run a normal week there
items.body: Keep Kumospace until the week is up, then decide which one the team actually opened.

workadventure.title: Why small teams look for a WorkAdventure alternative

items.title: Free rooms are public
items.body: WorkAdventure says its free plan's rooms are open to anyone with the link. Members, roles and limiting entry to certain email addresses come with the paid plans.

items.title: A world to build first
items.body: Templates get you started, but the map is yours to arrange, and a custom one is often a job for a designer. Some teams just want to walk in.

items.title: Self-hosting is a project
items.body: Running WorkAdventure on your own servers gives you full control, and it also means someone on the team keeps it up and updated.

items.title: Paying for capacity
items.body: Business is priced for how many people can be online at once, so you choose a number and pay for it, and change it as the team grows.

items.title: A world of your own
items.body: A map editor, templates, personalised desks and avatars, and a design team you can hire for a custom map. TinyFloor has one ready-made office.

items.title: Open source and self-hosting
items.body: You can run it on your own servers or private cloud and keep your data there. TinyFloor is hosted only.

items.title: Events and conferences
items.body: Speaker zones where only the speaker is heard, day pricing for one-off events, recording and live streaming to YouTube.

items.title: Integrations
items.body: Paid plans connect Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar and Google Meet, and there are AI bots and webhooks.

items.title: A bigger free plan
items.body: Ten people at once, with no time limit, is one of the roomiest free plans among the virtual offices we compared, if public rooms are fine for you.

items.title: TinyFloor, for a ready office
items.body: For a team of 4 to 15 that wants a private office it can open today, with desks, a meeting room and chat, for one price instead of a count of seats.

items.title: WorkAdventure, for your own world
items.body: If you want to design the space, host it yourself, run events in it, or connect it to Microsoft Teams or Google Calendar.

items.title: WorkAdventure free, for an open space
items.body: If public rooms are fine and you're 10 or fewer online at once, the free plan may be all you need.

items.title: Make an office
items.body: Name it after the team. The floor, desks and meeting room are ready; there's no map to carry over.

items.title: Share one invite link
items.body: Teammates sign in with Google or email and walk in from the browser, on a laptop or a phone.

items.title: Run a normal week there
items.body: Keep your WorkAdventure world until the week is up, then decide which one the team actually opened.
